doc.title: Kenny Davern interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 16, 2001 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Bandstand signals: whole notes, the bridge and Red Allen's 'George Washington'
summary: Rowe asks about hand signals; Davern explains them and tells of Red Allen's 'George Washington' bridge call confusing a Cleveland band.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: The whole — oh what’s the word I’m looking for — the kind of thing that happens on the bandstand, the etiquette, is really interesting to watch, even besides the music. You know, who solos when and all that. I really find that fascinating to watch. And you did something last night, I was watching from outside the window, I think it was last night, that I had never seen before. Somebody was soloing, and it was coming to the bridge and you went like this.
I had never seen that particular gesture before, and everybody knew what to do. Just play whole notes as a background.
Is that something that’s been, I mean that and all those other things have been around for—
Everybody has their different signals you know. This means back to the bridge.

Right. Or it could mean, in some instances, theme song. The T. But in a jazz band, that would mean bridge in some circles. An example of how that could get screwed up was Henry “Red” Allen, who loved to work in a quartet format, went out to Detroit to play a club, no it was Cleveland. Went to Cleveland to play the Theatrical Lounge. And he had locals. And he was playing a tune, “Rosetta” or whatever it was, and he wanted to take it out. So he yells, “George Washington.” And you know the band comes back and finishes the last date and it goes right back to the head or the top, and he’s at the bridge. Complete train wreck. When it was all over and everybody sort of caught up to each other he says, “I told you George Washington” and he looked at everybody “what the fuck is George Washington?” He says, “The bridge, the bridge.” Well they’d never heard of the George
Washington bridge in Cleveland. So there, Monk, is an example of how that completely turned around.
I heard Claude “Fiddler” Williams once, he goes “channel.”
He called it channel, I had never heard that.
I have heard the channel, yeah. Channel, you know, the channel. Under the water. Over the water, whatever. The bridge, same thing. Channel, under, bridge, over. George Washington.
